newsitem.title: BRAZIL: No cocoa buyers in Brazil despite small crop.
newsitem.headline: No cocoa buyers in Brazil despite small crop.

text.p: The Brazilian cocoa market was in a bizarre state this week with farmers and dealers unable to find buyers for cocoa beans even though the crop is one of the smallest on record, traders said.
"We have what is almost certainly a record low crop for the last 20 years and yet people don't want to buy," said a trader.

"Everyone, myself included, believed that by this stage of the crop, prices would be shooting up and there would a scramble to buy cocoa but instead they've dropped. We have beans and we can't sell them."
"The market is dead. There are no buyers for cocoa at all. I've never seen anything like it. In the past, there was always someone who would pick something up even during the quiet times."

Traders said that as a result of the lull in demand, internal prices had slumped from 21 Real per 15-kilo arroba at the end of last year to only 18 Real this week. A further drop was on the cards next week, traders said.

This was the first drop in internal prices since October, when a new law abolishing a sales tax on exported cocoa was introduced, giving farmers -- who had effectively paid the tax -- a rise of 15 to 20 percent overnight.

Traders said the current main crop, which runs from October to April, was expected to yield only 1 million 60-kilo bags after a two-month drought struck during the flowering period in July and August.

But the four local grinders had anticipated the shortage and built up stocks which would last them until Easter, traders said. This, combined with the fact that Bahia is no longer a regular exporter of cocoa, had combined to produce the current state of affairs.

"They have three or four months' supply and, given that they normally close for a couple of weeks for maintenance anyway, that should take them through until the start of the main crop," said a trader.
Traders said that the cocoa growing region had escaped the heavy rains which brought flooding to parts of south-eastern Brazil in the last week.
"We have only had around one tenth of that rainfall in the region," said one.
They said the next midcrop, which starts in May, was developing well, although allowances would have to be made for the inevitable losses which will be caused by witch's broom disease.
